div.p: [To those who follow him.] Hush! [To Rose.] I
discovered 'em clustered in the doorway——

[There is a final peal of thunder as Avonia, Gadd, Colpoys, and Tom Wrench enter, somewhat diffidently. They are apparently soaked to their skins, and are altogether in a deplorable condition. Avonia alone has an umbrella, which she allows to drip upon the carpet, but her dress and petticoats are bedraggled, her finery limp, her hair lank and loose.]

div.head: Rose.
div.p: 'Vonia!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Coming to her, and embracing her fervently.] Oh, ducky, ducky, ducky! oh, but what a storm!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Hush! how wet you are! [Shaking hands with Gadd] Ferdinand—[crossing to Colpoys and shaking hands with him] Augustus—[shaking hands with Tom] Tom-Wrench—

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [To Charles.] Be so kind as to put my umbrella on the landing, will you? Oh, thank you very much, I'm sure.
[Charles withdraws with the umbrella. Gadd and Colpoys shake the rain from their hats on to the carpet and furniture.]

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Quietly, to Rose.] It's a shame to come down on you in this way. But they would do it, and I thought I'd better stick to 'em.
Gadd.
[Who is a little flushed and unsteady.] Ha! I shall remember this accursed evening.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Oh, Ferdy——!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Hush! you must be quiet. Everybody has gone to bed, and I—I'm not sure I'm allowed to receive visitors——

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Oh!

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: Then we are intruders?

div.head: Rose.
div.p: I mean, such late visitors.
[Colpoys has taken off his coat, and is shaking it vigorously.]

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Stop it, Augustus! ain't I wet enough? [To Rose.] Yes, it is latish, but I so wanted to inform you—here—[bringing Gadd forward] allow me to introduce —my husband.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Oh! no!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Laughing merrily.] Yes, ha, ha, ha!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Sssh, sssh, sssh!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: I forgot. [To Gadd.] Oh, darling Ferdy, you're positively soaked! [To Rose.] Do let him take his coat off, like Gussy——

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: [Jealously.] 'Vonia, not so much of the Gussy!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: There you are, flying out again I as if Mr. Colpoys wasn't an old friend!

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: Old friend or no old friend——

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Diplomatically.] Certainly, take your coat off, Ferdinand.
[Gadd joins Colpoys; they spread out their coats upon the couch.]

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Feeling Tom's coat sleeve.] And you?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [After glancing at the others—quietly.] No, thank you.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Sitting.] Yes, dearie, Ferdy and I were married yesterday.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Sitting. ] Yesterday!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Yesterday morning. We're on our honeymoon now. You know, the "Wells" shut a fortnight after you left us, and neither Ferdy nor me could fix anything, just for the present, elsewhere; and as we hadn't put by during the season—you know it never struck us to put by during the season—we thought we'd get married.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Oh, yes.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: You see, a man and his wife can live almost on what keeps one, rent and ceterer; and so, being deeply attached, as I tell you, we went off to church and did the deed. Oh, it will be such a save. [Looking up at Gadd coyly.] Oh, Ferdy———!

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: [Laying his hand upon her head, dreamily.] Yes, child, I confess I love you—.
Colpoys
[Behind Rose, imitating Gadd.] Child, I confess I adore you.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Taking Colpoys by the arm and swinging him away from Rose.] Enough of that, Colpoys!

div.head: Colpoys.
div.p: What!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Rising.] Hush!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Under his breath.] If you've never learnt how to behave——

div.head: Colpoys.
div.p: Don't you teach behavior, sir, to a gentleman who plays a superior line of business to yourself! [Muttering. ] 'Pon my soul! rum start!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Going to Rose.] Of course I ought to have written to you, dear, properly, but you remember the weeks it takes me to write a letter—- [Gadd sits in the chair Avonia has just quitted; she returns and seats herself upon his knee.]And so I said to Ferdy, over tea, "Ferdy, let's spend a bit of our honeymoon' in doing the West End thoroughly, and going and seeing where Rose Trelawny lives." And we thought it only nice and polite to invite Tom Wrench and Gussy——

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: 'Vonia, much less of the Gussy!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Kissing Gadd.] Jealous boy! [Beaming.] Oh, and we have done the West End thoroughly. There, I've never done the West End so thoroughly in my life! And when we got outside your house I couldn't resist. [Her hand on Gadd's shirt sleeve.] Oh, gracious! I'm sure you'll catch your death, my darling—-!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: I think I can get him some wine. [To Gadd.] Will you take some wine, Ferdinand?
[Gadd rises, nearly upsetting Avonia.]

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Ferdy!

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: I thank you. [ With a wave of the hand.] Anything, anything——

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [To Rose.] Anything that goes with stout, dear.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [At the door, turning to them.] 'Vonia—boys—be very still.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Trust us!
[Rose tiptoes out. Colpoys is now at the card-table, cutting a pack of cards which remains there.]

div.head: Colpoys.
div.p: [To Gadd.] Gadd, I'll see you for pennies.

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: [Loftily.] Done, sir, with you!
[They seat themselves at the table, and cut for coppers. Tom is walking about, surveying the room.]

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Taking off her hat and wiping it with her handkerchief.] Well, Thomas, what do you think of it?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: This is the kind of chamber I want for the first act of my comedy——-

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Oh, lor', your head's continually running on your comedy. Half this blessed evening——

div.head: Tom.
div.p: I tell you, I won't have doors stuck here, there, and everywhere; no, nor windows in all sorts of impossible places!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Oh, really! Well, when you do get your play accepted, mind you see that Mr. Manager gives you exactly what you ask for—won't you?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: You needn't be satirical, if you are wet. Yes, I will I [Pointing to the left.] Windows on the one side [pointing to the right], doors on the other—just where they should be, architecturally. And locks on the doors, real locks, to work; and handles—to turn! [Rubbing his hands together gleefully.] Ha, ha! you wait! wait—!
[Rose re-enters, with a plate of biscuits in her hand, followed by Charles, who carries a decanter of sherry and some wine-glasses.]

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Here, Charles——-
[Charles places the decanter and the glasses on the table.]

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: [Whose luck has been against him, throwing himself, sulkily, onto the couch.] Bah! I'll risk no further stake.

div.head: Colpoys.
div.p: Just because you lose sevenpence in coppers you go on like this!
[Charles, turning from the table, faces Colpoys.]
======== below this needs correction ==

div.head: Colpoys.
div.p: [Tearing his hair, and glaring at Charles wildly.] Ah—h—h, I am ruined! I have lost my all! my children are beggars——!

div.head: Charles.
div.p: Ho, ho, ho! he, he, he!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Hush, hush! [Charles goes out laughing. To everybody;]Sherry?

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: [Rising.] Sherry!
[Avonia, Colpoys; and Gadd gather round the table, and help themselves to sherry and biscuits.]

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [To Tom.] Tom, won't you——-?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Watching Gadd anxiously.] No, thank you. The fact is, we—we have already partaken of refreshments, once or twice during the evening——
[Colpoys and Avonia, each carrying a glass of wine and munching a biscuit, go to the couch, where they sit.]

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: [Pouring out sherry—singing.] "And let me the canakin clink, clink—-"

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Coming to him.] Be quiet, Gadd!

div.head: Colpoys.
div.p: [Raising his glass.] The Bride!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Turning, kissing her hand to Avonia.] Yes, yes [Gadd hands Rose his glass; she puts her lips to it.] The Bride!
[She returns the glass to Gadd.]

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: [Sitting.] My bride!
[Tom, from behind the table, unperceived, takes the decanter and hides it under the table, then sits. Gadd, missing the decanter, contents himself with the biscuits.]

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Well, Rose, my darling, we've been talking about nothing but ourselves. How are you getting along here?

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Getting along? oh, I—I don't fancy I'm getting along very well, thank you!

div.head: Colpoys. and Avonia.
div.p: Not——!

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: [His mouth full of biscuit.] Not——!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Sitting by the card-table.] No, boys; no 'Vonia. The truth is, it isn't as nice as you'd think it. I suppose the Profession had its drawbacks—mother used to say so—but [raising her arms] one could fly. Yes, in Brydon Crescent one was a dirty little London sparrow, perhaps; but here, in this grand square——! Oh, it's the story of the caged bird, over again.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: A love-bird, though.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Poor Arthur? yes, he's a dear. [Rising.] But the Gowers—the old Gowers! the Gowers! the Gowers I [She paces the room, beating her hands together. In her excitement, she ceases to whisper, and gradually becomes loud and voluble. The others, following her leady chatter noisily—excepting Tom, who sits thoughtfully, looking before him.]

div.head: Rose.
div.p: The ancient Gowers! the venerable Gowers!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: You mean, the grandfather——-?

div.head: Rose.
div.p: And the aunt—the great-aunt—the great bore of a great-aunt! The very mention of 'em makes something go "tap, tap, tap, tap" at the top of my head.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Oh, I am sorry to hear this. Well, upon my word——!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Would you believe it? 'Vonia—boys—you'll never believe it! I mayn't walk out with Arthur alone, nor see him here alone. I mayn't sing; no, nor sneeze even——

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Shrilly.]Not sing or sneeze!

div.head: Colpoys.
div.p: [Indignantly. ] Not sneeze!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: No, nor sit on the floor—the floor!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Why, when we shared rooms together, you were always on the floor!

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: [Producing a pipe, and knocking out the ashes on the heel of his boot.] In Heaven's name, what kind of house can this be!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: I wouldn't stand it, would you, Ferdinand?

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: [Loading his pipe.] Gad, no!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [To Colpoys.] Would you, Gus, dear?

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: [Under his breath.] Here! not so much of the Gus dear——

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [To Colpoys.] Would you?

div.head: Colpoys.
div.p: No, I'm blessed if I would, my darling.

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: [His pipe in his mouth.] Mr. Colpoys! less of the darling!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Rising.] Rose, don't you put up with it! [Striking the top of the card-table vigorously.] I say, don't you stand it! [Embracing Rose.] You're an independent girl, dear; they came to you, these people; not you to them, remember.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Sitting on the couch.] Oh, what can I do? I can't do anything.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Can't you! [Coming to Gadd.] Ferdinand, advise her. You tell her how to——

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: [Who has risen.] Miss Bunn—Mrs. Gadd, you have been all over Mr. Colpoys this evening, ever since we——

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Angrily, pushing him back into his chair.] Oh, don't be a silly!

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: Madam!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Returning to Colpoys.] Gus, Ferdinand's foolish. Come and talk to Rose, and advise her, there's a dear boy——
[Colpoys rises; she takes his arm, to lead him to Rose. At that moment Gadd advances to Colpoys and slaps his face violently.]

div.head: Colpoys.
div.p: Hey——!

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: Miserable viper!

[The two men close. Tom runs to separate them. Rose rises with a cry of terror. There is a struggle and general uproar. The card-table is overturned, with a crash, and Avonia utters a long and piercing shriek. Then the house-bells are heard ringing violently.]

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Oh——! [The combatants part; all look scared. At the door, listening.] They are moving—coming! Turn out the——!

[She turns out the light at the table. The room is in half-light as Sir William enters, cautiously, closely followed by Miss Gower. They are both in dressing-gowns and slippers; Sir William carries a thick stick and his bedroom candle. Rose is standing by a chair; Gadd, Avonia, Colpoys, and Tom are together.]

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Miss Trelawny——!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: ——! [Running behind the screen.] Men!

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Who are these people?

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Advancing a step or two.] Some friends of mine who used to be at the "Wells" have called upon me, to inquire how I am getting on.
[Arthur enters, quickly.]

div.head: Arthur.
div.p: [Looking round.] Oh! Rose——!

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Turning upon him.] Ah—h—h—h! How come you here?

div.head: Arthur.
div.p: I was outside the house. Charles let me in, knowing something was wrong.

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Peering into his face.] Troubadouring-?

div.head: Arthur.
div.p: Troubadouring; yes, sir. [To Rose.] Rose, what is this?

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Fiercely.] No, sir, this is my affair. [Placing his candlestick on the table.] Stand aside! [Raising his stick furiously.] Stand aside!
[Arthur moves to the right.]

div.head: Miss Gower.
div.p: [Over the screen.] William——

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Hey?

div.head: Miss Gower.
div.p: Your ankles—-

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Adjusting his dressing-gown.] I beg your pardon. [To Arthur.] Yes, I can answer your question. [Painting his stick, first at Rose, then at the group.] Some friends of that young woman's connected with—the playhouse, have favored us with a visit, for the purpose of ascertaining how she is—getting on. [Touching Gadd's pipe, which is lying at his feet, with the end of his stick.] A filthy tobacco-pipe. To whom does it belong? whose is it?
[Rose picks it up and passes it to Gadd, bravely.]

div.head: Rose.
div.p: It belongs to one of my friends.

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Taking Gadd's empty wine-glass and holding it to his nose.] Phu, yes! In brief, a drunken debauch. [To the group.] So ye see, gentlemen—[to Avonia] and you, madam; [to Arthur] and you, sir; you see, all of ye, [sinking into a chair, and coughing from exhaustion] exactly how Miss Trelawny is getting on.

div.head: Miss Gower.
div.p: [Over the screen.] William——

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: What is it?

div.head: Miss Gower.
div.p: Your ankles—-

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Leaping to his feet, in a frenzy.] Bah!

div.head: Miss Gower.
div.p: Oh, they seem so out of place!

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Flourishing his stick—to the group down L. ] Begone! a set of garish, dissolute gypsies! begone!
[Gadd, Avonia, Colpoys, and Wrench gather, the men hastily putting on their coats, etc.]

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Where's my umbrella?

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: A hand with my coat here!

div.head: Colpoys.
div.p: 'Pon my soul! London artists——!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: We don't want to remain where we're not heartily welcome, I can assure everybody.

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Open windows! let in the air!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [To Rose, who is standing above the wreck of the card-table.] Good-bye, my dear——

div.head: Rose.
div.p: No, no, 'Vonia. Oh, don't leave me behind you!

div.head: Arthur.
div.p: Rose.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Oh, I'm very sorry, Arthur. [To Sir William.] Indeed, I am very sorry, Sir William. But you are right—gypsies—gypsies! [To Arthur.] Yes, Arthur, if you were a gypsy, as I am, as these friends o' mine are, we might be happy together. But I've seen enough of your life, my dear boy, to know that I'm no wife for you. I should only be wretched, and would make you wretched; and the end, when it arrived, as it very soon would, would be much as it is to-night-!

div.head: Arthur.
div.p: [Distractedly.] You'll let me see you, talk to you, to-morrow, Rose?

div.head: Rose.
div.p: No, never!

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Sharply.] You mean that?

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Facing him.] Oh, don't be afraid. I give you my word.

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Gripping her hand.] Thank ye. Thank ye.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Quietly to Arthur.] Mr. Gower, come and see me to morrow——- [He moves away to the door.]

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Turning to Avonia, Gadd, and Colpoys.] I'm ready——

div.head: Miss Gower.
div.p: [Coming from behind the screen to the back of the couch.] Not to-night, child! not to-night! where will you go?

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Holding Rose.] To her old quarters in Brydon Crescent. Send her things after her, if you please.

div.head: Miss Gower.
div.p: And then——?

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Then back to the "Wells" again, Miss Gower! back to the "Wells"——!

div.head: THE THIRD ACT.

p.hi: The scene represents an apartment on the second floor of Mrs. Mossop's house. The room is of a humbler character than that shown in the first act; but, though shabby, it is neat. On the right is a door, outside which is supposed to be the landing. In the wall at the back is another door, presumably admitting to a further chamber. Down L. there is a fireplace, with a fire burning, and over the mantelpiece a mirror. In the left-hand corner of the room is a small bedstead with a tidily-made bed, which can be hidden by a pair of curtains of some common and faded material, hanging from a cord slung from wall to wall. At the foot of the bedstead stands a large theatrical dress-basket. On the wall, by the head of the bed, are some pegs upon which hang a skirt or two and other articles of attire. On the right, against the back wall, there is a chest of drawers, the top of which is used as a washstand. In front of this is a small screen, and close by there are some more pegs with things hanging upon them. On the right wall, above the sofa, is a hanging bookcase with a few books. A small circular table, with a somewhat shabby cover upon it, stands on the left. The walls are papered, the doors painted stone-color. An old felt carpet is on the floor. The light is that of morning. A fire is burning in the grate.

div.p: [Mrs. Mossop, now dressed in a workaday gown, has just finished making the bed. There is a knock at the center door.]

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [From the adjoining room.] Rose!

div.head: Mrs. Mossop.
div.p: [Giving a final touch to the quilt.] Eh?

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Is Miss Trelawny in her room?

div.head: Mrs. Mossop.
div.p: No, Mrs. Gadd; she's at rehearsal.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Oh——

[Mrs. Mossop draws the curtains, hiding the bed from view. Avonia enters by the door on the right in a morning wrapper which has seen its best days. She carries a pair of curling-tongs, and her hair is evidently in process of being dressed in ringlets.]

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Of course she is; I forgot. There's a call for The Peddler of Marseilles. Thank Gawd, I'm not in it. [Singing.] "I'm a great guerrilla chief, I'm a robber and a thief, I can either kill a foe or prig a pocket-handkerchief——"

div.head: Mrs. Mossop.
div.p: [Dusting the ornaments on the mantelpiece.] Bless your heart, you're very gay this morning!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: It's the pantomime. I'm always stark mad as the pantomime approaches. I don't grudge letting the rest of the company have their fling at other times—but with the panto comes my turn. [Throwing herself full length upon the sofa gleefully.]Ha, ha, ha! the turn of Avonia Bunn! [__With a change of tone.__] I hope Miss Trelawny won't take a walk up to Highbury, or anywhere, after rehearsal. I want to borrow her gilt belt. My dress has arrived.

div.head: Mrs. Mossop.
div.p: [Much interested.] No! has it?

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Yes, Mrs. Burroughs is coming down from the theatre at twelve-thirty to see me in it. [Singing. "Any kind of villainy cometh natural to me. So it endeth with a combat and a one, two, three——!"] *

div.head: Mrs. Mossop.
div.p: [Surveying the room.] Well, that's as cheerful as I can make things look, poor dear!
* These snatches of song are from "The Miller and His Men," a burlesque mealy-drama, by Francis Talfourd and Henry J. Byron, produced at the Strand Theatre, April 9, 1860.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Taking a look round, seriously.] It's pretty bright—if it wasn't for the idea of Rose Trelawny having to economize!

div.head: Mrs. Mossop.
div.p: Ah—h I

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Rising.] That's what I can't swallow. [Sticking her irons in the fire angrily.] One room! and on the second floor! [Turning to Mrs. Mossop.] Of course, Gadd and me are one-room people too—and on the same floor; but then Gadd is so popular out of the theatre, Mrs. Mossop—he's obliged to spend such a load of money at the "Clown"——

div.head: Mrs. Mossop.
div.p: [Who has been dusting the bookcase, coming to the table.] Mrs. Gadd, dearie, I'm sure I'm not in the least inquisitive; no one could accuse me of it—but I should like to know just one thing.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Testing her irons upon a sheet of paper which she takes from the table.] What's that?

div.head: Mrs. Mossop.
div.p: Why have they been and cut down Miss Trelawny's salary at the "Wells"?

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Hesitatingly.] H'm, everybody's chattering about it; you could get to hear easily enough——

div.head: Mrs. Mossop.
div.p: Oh, I dare say.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: So I don't mind—poor Rose! they tell her she can't act now, Mrs. Mossop.

div.head: Mrs. Mossop.
div.p: Can't act!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: No, dear old girl, she's lost it; it's gone from her—the trick of it——
[Tom enters by the door on the right, carrying a table-cover of a bright pattern.]

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Coming upon Mrs. Mossop, disconcerted.] Oh——!

div.head: Mrs. Mossop.
div.p: My first-floor table-cover!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Y—y—yes. [Exchanging the table-covers.] I thought, as the Telfers have departed, and as their late sitting room is at present vacant, that Miss Trelawny might enjoy the benefit—hey?

div.head: Mrs. Mossop.
div.p: [Snatching up the old table-cover.] Well, I never—-! [She goes out.]

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Curling her hair, at the mirror over the mantelpiece.] I say, Tom, I wonder if I've done wrong——

div.head: Tom.
div.p: It all depends upon whether you've had the chance.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: I've told Mrs. Mossop the reason they've reduced Rose's salary.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: You needn't.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: She had only to ask any other member of the company——-

div.head: Tom.
div.p: To have found one who could have kept silent!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Remorsefully.] Oh, I could burn myself!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Besides, it isn't true.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: What?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: That Rose Trelawny is no longer up to her work.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Sadly.] Oh, Tom!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: It isn't the fact, I say!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Isn't it the fact that ever since Rose returned from Cavendish Square——?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: She has been reserved, subdued, ladylike——

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Shrilly.]She was always ladylike!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: I'm aware of that!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Well, then, what do you mean by—?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [In a rage, turning away.] Oh——!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Heating her irons again.] The idea!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Cooling down.] She was always a ladylike actress, on the stage and off it, but now she has developed into a—[at a loss] into a——

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Scornfully.] Ha!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Into a ladylike human being. These fools at the "Wells"! Can't act, can't she! No, she can no longer spout, she can no longer ladle, the vapid trash, the—the—the turgid rodomontade——

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Doubtfully.] You'd better be careful of your language, Wrench.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [With a twinkle in his eye—mopping his brow.] You're a married woman, 'Vonia——

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Holding her irons to her cheek, modestly.] I know, but still——

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Yes, deep down in the well of that girl's nature there has been lying a little, bright, clear pool of genuine refinement, girlish simplicity. And now the bucket has been lowered by love; experience has turned the handle; and up comes the crystal to the top, pure and sparkling. Why, her broken engagement to poor young Gower has really been the making of her! It has transformed her! Can't act, can't she! [__Drawing a long breath.__] How she would play Dora in my comedy!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Ho, that comedy!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: How she would murmur those love-scenes!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Murder——!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Testily.] Murmur. [Partly to himself.] Do you know, 'Vonia, I had Rose in my mind when I imagined Dora——?

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Ha, ha! you astonish me.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Sitting.] And Arthur Gower when I wrote the character of Gerald, Dora's lover. [In a low voice.] Gerald and Dora—Rose and Arthur—Gerald and Dora. [Suddenly.] 'Vonia——!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Singeing her hair.] Ah—! oh, lor'! what now?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: I wish you could keep a secret.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Why, can't I?——

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Haven't you just been gossiping with Mother Mossop?

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Behind his chair, breathlessly, her eyes bolting.]
A secret, Tom?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Nodding.] I should like to share it with you, because—you are fond of her too——

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Ah——!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: And because the possession of it is worrying me. But there, I can't trust you.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Mr. Wrench!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: No, you're a warm-hearted woman, 'Vonia, but you're a sieve.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Going down upon her knees beside him.] I swear! By all my hopes, Tom Wrench, of hitting 'em as Prince Charming in the coming pantomime, I swear I will not divulge, leave alone tell a living soul, any secret you may intrust to me, or let me know of, concerning Rose Trelawny of the "Wells." Amen!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [In her ear.] 'Vonia, I know where Arthur Gower is.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Is! isn't he still in London?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Producing a letter mysteriously.] No. When Rose stuck to her refusal to see him—listen—mind, not a word——!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: By all my hopes——-!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Checking her]. All right, all right! [Reading.] "Theatre Royal, Bristol. Friday————-"

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Theatre Royal, Br——!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Be quiet! [Reading.] "My dear Mr. Wrench. A whole week, and not a line from you to tell me how Miss Trelawny is. When you are silent I am sleepless at night and a haggard wretch during the day. Young Mr. Kirby, our Walking Gentleman, has been unwell, and the management has given me temporarily some of his business to play———"

div.head: Arthur.
div.p: Gower———!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Will you? [Reading.] "Last night I was allowed to appear as Careless in The School for Scandal. Miss Mason, the Lady Teazle, complimented me, but the men said I lacked vigor,"—the old cry!—"and so this morning I am greatly depressed. But I will still persevere, as long as you can assure me that no presuming fellow is paying attention to Miss Trelawny. Oh, how badly she treated me——!"

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Following the reading of the letter.] "How badly she treated me——!"

div.head: Tom.
div.p: "I will never forgive her—only love her——"

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: "Only love her——"

div.head: Tom.
div.p: "Only love her, and hope I may some day become a great actor, and, like herself, a gypsy. Yours very gratefully, Arthur Gordon."

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: In the Profession!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Bolted from Cavendish Square—went down to Bristol——

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: How did he manage it all? [Tom taps his breast proudly.] But isn't Rose to be told? why shouldn't she be told?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: She has hurt the boy, stung him to the quick, and he's proud.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: But she loves him now that she believes he has forgotten her. She only half loved him before. She loves him!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Serve her right.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Oh, Tom, is she never to know?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Folding the letter carefully.] Some day, when he begins to make strides.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Strides! he's nothing but General Utility at present?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Putting the letter in his pocket.] No.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: And how long have you been that?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Ten years.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [With a little screech.] Ah—h—h! she ought to be told!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Seizing her wrist.] Woman, you won't——!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Raising her disengaged hand.] By all my hopes of hitting 'em——!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: All right, I believe you. [Listening.] Sssh!
[They rise and separate, he moving to the fire, she to the right, as Rose enters. Rose is now a grave, dignified, somewhat dreamy young woman.]

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Looking from Tom to Avonia.] Ah——?

div.head: Tom. and Avonia.
div.p: Good-morning.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Kissing Avonia.] Visitors!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: My fire's so black [showing her irons]; I thought you wouldn't mind——

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Removing her gloves.] Of course not. [Seeing the table-cover.] Oh——!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Mrs. Mossop. asked me to bring that upstairs. It was in the Telfers' room, you know, and she fancied——-

div.head: Rose.
div.p: How good of her! thanks, Tom. [Taking off her hat and mantle.] Poor Mr. and Mrs. Telfer! they still wander mournfully about the "Wells"; they can get nothing to do.
[Carrying her hat and umbrella, she disappears through the curtains.]

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [To Avonia, in a whisper, across the room.] The Telfers——!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Eh?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: She's been giving 'em money.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Yes.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Damn!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Reappearing.] What are yous saying about me.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: I was wondering whether you'd lend me that belt you bought for Ophelia; to wear during the first two or three weeks of the pantomime—-

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Certainly, 'Vonia, to wear throughout——

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Embracing her.] No, it's too good; I'd rather fake one for the rest of the time. [Looking into her face.] What's the matter?

div.head: Rose.
div.p: I will make you a present of the belt, 'Vonia, if you will accept it. I bought it when I came back to the "Wells," thinking everything would go on as before. But—it's of no use; they tell me I cannot act effectively any longer——

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Indignantly. ] Effectively——!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: First, as you know, they reduce my salary——-

div.head: Tom. and Avonia.
div.p: [With clenched hands.] Yes!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: And now, this morning—[sitting] you can guess——

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Hoarsely.] Got your notice?

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Yes.

div.head: Tom. and Avonia.
div.p: Oh—h—h!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [After a litle pause.] Poor mother! I hope she doesn't see. [Overwhelmed, Avonia and Tom sit.] I was running through Blanche, my old part in The Peddler of Marseilles, when Mr. Burroughs spoke to me. It is true I was doing it tamely, but—it is such nonsense.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Hear, hear!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: And then, that poor little song I used to sing on the bridge—-

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Singing softly.] "Ever of thee I'm fondly-dreaming——-"

div.head: Tom. and Avonia.
div.p: [Singing.] "Thy gentle voice my spirit can cheer."

div.head: Rose.
div.p: I told Mr. Burroughs I should cut it out. So ridiculously inappropriate!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: And that—did it?

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Smiling at him.] That did it.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Kneeling beside her, and embracing her tearfully.] My ducky! oh, but there are other theatres besides the "Wells"——-

div.head: Rose.
div.p: For me? only where the same trash is acted.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [With a sob.] But a few months ago you l—l—liked your work.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Yes [dreamily], and then I went to Cavendish Square, engaged to Arthur——[Tom rises and leans upon the mantelpiece, looking into the fire.] How badly I behaved in Cavendish Square! how unlike a young lady! What if the old folks were overbearing and tyrannical, Arthur could be gentle with them. "They have not many more years in this world," he said—dear boy!—"and anything we can do to make them happy——" And what did I do? There was a chance for me—to be patient, and womanly; and I proved to them that I was nothing but—an actress.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Rising, hurt but still tearful.] It doesn't follow, because one is a—-

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Rising.] Yes, 'Vonia, it does! We are only dolls, partly human, with mechanical limbs that will fall into stagey postures, and heads stuffed with sayings out of rubbishy plays. It isn't the world we live in, merely a world—such a queer little one! I was less than a month in Cavendish Square, and very few people came there; but they were real people—real! For a month I lost the smell of gas and oranges, and the hurry and noise, and the dirt and the slang, and the clownish joking, at the "Wells." I didn't realize at the time the change that was going on in me; I didn't realize it till I came back. And then, by degrees, I discovered what had happened——
[Tom is now near her. She takes his hand and drops her head upon Avonia's shoulder. Wearily.]
Oh, Tom! oh, 'Vonia———[From the next room comes the sound of the throwing about of heavy objects, and of Gadd's voice uttering loud imprecations. Alarmed.] Oh——!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Listening attentively.] Sounds like Ferdy. [She goes to the center door. At the keyhole.] Ferdy! aint you well, darling?

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: [On the other side of the door.]Avonia!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: I'm in Miss Trelawny's room.

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: Ah!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [To Rose and Tom.] Now, what's put Ferdy out? [Gadd enters with a wild look.] Ferdinand!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Anything wrong, Gadd?

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: Wrong! wrong! [Sitting.] What d'ye think?

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Tell us!

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: I have been asked to appear in the pantomime.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Shocked.] Oh, Ferdy! you!

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: I, a serious actor, if ever there was one; a poetic actor——!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: What part, Ferdy?

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: The insult, the bitter insult! the gross indignity!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: What part, Ferdy?

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: I have not been seen in pantomime for years, not since I shook the dust of the T. R. Stockton from my feet.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Ferdy, what part?

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: I simply looked at Burroughs, when he preferred his request, and swept from the theatre.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: What part, Ferdy?

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: A part, too, which is seen for a moment at the opening of the pantomime, and not again till its close.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Ferdy.

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: Eh?

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: What part?

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: A character called the Demon of Discontent.
[Rose turns away to the fireplace; Tom curls himself up on the sofa and is seen to shake with laughter.]

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Walking about indignantly.]Oh! [Returning to Gadd.] Oh, it's a rotten part! Rose, dear, I assure you, as artist to artist, that part is absolutely rotten. [To Gadd.] You won't play it, darling?

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: [Rising.] Play it! I would see the "Wells" in ashes first.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: We shall lose our engagements, Ferdy. I know Burroughs; we shall be out, both of us.

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: Of course we shall. D'ye think I have not counted the cost?

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Putting her hand in his.] I don't mind, dear—for the sake of your position—[struck by a sudden thought] oh!

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: What——-?

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: There now—we haven't put by!
[There is a knock at the door.]

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Who is that?

div.head: Colpoys.
div.p: [Outside the door.] Is Gadd here, Miss Trelawny?

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Yes.

div.head: Colpoys.
div.p: I want to see him.

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: Wrench, I'll trouble you. Ask Mr. Colpoys whether he approaches me as a friend, an acquaintance, or in his capacity of stage manager at the "Wells"—the tool of Burroughs.
[Tom opens the door slightly. Gadd and Avonia join Bose at the fireplace.]

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [At the door, solemnly.]Colpoys, are you here as Gadd's bosom friend, or as a mere tool of Burroughs?
[An inaudible colloquy follows between Tom and Colpoys. Tom's head is outside the door; his legs are seen to move convulsively, and the sound of suppressed laughter is heard.]

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: [Turning.] Well, well?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Closing the door sharply, and facing Gadd with great seriousness.] He is here as the tool of Burroughs.

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: I will receive him.
[Tom admits Colpoys, who carries a mean-looking "part," and a letter.]
[After formally bowing to the ladies.] Oh, Gadd, Mr. Burroughs instructs me to offer you this part in the pantomime. [Handing the part to Gadd.] Demon of Discontent.
[Gadd takes the part and flings it to the ground; Avonia picks it up and reads it.]

div.head: Colpoys.
div.p: You refuse it?

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: I do. [With dignity.] Acquaint Mr. Burroughs with my decision, and add that I hope his pantomime will prove an utterly mirthless one. May Boxing-night, to those unfortunate enough to find themselves in the theatre, long remain a dismal memory; and may succeeding audiences, scanty and dissatisfied——! [Colpoys presents Gadd with the letter. Gadd opens it and reads.] I leave. [Sitting.] The Romeo, the Orlando, the Clifford—leaves!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Coming to Gadd, indicating some lines in the part.] Ferdy, this aint so bad. [Reading.]
"I'm Discontent! from Orkney's isle to Dover
To make men's bile bile-over I endover-"

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: 'Vonia! [Taking the part from Avonia, with mingled surprise and pleasure.] Ho, ho! no, that's not bad. [Reading.]
Tempers, though sweet, I whip up to a lather,
Make wives hate husbands, sons wish fathers farther."
'Vonia, there's is something to lay hold of here! I'll think this over. [Rising, addressing Colpoys.] Gus, I have thought this over. I play it.
[They all gather round him, and congratulate him. Avonia embraces and kisses him.]

div.head: Tom. and Colpoys.
div.p: That's right!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: I'm very pleased, Ferdinand.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Tearfully.] Oh, Ferdy!

div.head: Gadd.
div.p: [In high spirits.] Egad, I play it! Gus, I'll stroll back with you to the "Wells." [Shaking hands with Rose.] Miss Trelawny———-! [Avonia accompanies Colpoys and Gadd to the door, clinging to Gadd, who is flourishing the part.] 'Vonia, I see myself in this! [Kissing her.] Steak for dinner!
[Gadd and Colpoys go out. Tom shrieks with laughter.]

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Turning upon him, angrily and volubly.]Yes, I heard you with Colpoys outside that door, if Gadd didn't. It's a pity, Mr. Wrench, you can't find something better to do——!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Pacifically.] Hush, hush, 'Vonia! Tom, assist me with my basket; I'll give 'Vonia her belt——
[Tom and Rose go behind the curtains and presently emerge, carrying the dress-basket, which they deposit.]

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Flouncing across the room.] Making fun of Gadd! an artist to the roots of his hair! There's more talent in Gadd's little finger——!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Rummaging among the contents of the basket] 'Vonia, 'Vonia!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: And if Gadd is to play a demon in the pantomime, what do you figure as, Tom Wrench, among the half a dozen other things? Why, as part of a dragon! Yes, and which end—-?

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Quietly to Tom.] Apologize to 'Vonia at once, Tom.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Meekly.] Mrs. Gadd, I beg your pardon.

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Coming to him and kissing him.] Granted, Tom; but you should be a little more considerate——

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Holding up the belt.] Here——!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Taking the belt, ecstatically.] Oh, isn't it lovely! Rose, you dear! you sweet thing! [Singing a few bars of the Jewel song from Faust, then rushing at Rose and embracing her.] I'm going to try my dress on, to show Mrs. Burroughs. Come and help me into it. I'll unlock my door on my side——
[Tom politely opens the door for her to pass out.] Thank you, Tom—[kissing him again] only you should be more considerate toward Gadd——
[She disappears.]

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Calling after her.] I will be; I will—[Shutting the door.] Ha, ha, ha!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Smiling.] Hush! poor 'Vonia! [Mending the fire.] Excuse me, Tom—have you a fire upstairs, in your room, to-day?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Er—n—not to-day—it's Saturday. I never have a fire on a Saturday.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Coming to him.] Why not?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Looking away from her.] Don't know—creatures of habit—-

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Gently touching his coat-sleeve.] Because if you would like to smoke your pipe by my fire while I'm with 'Vonia——
[The key is heard to turn in the lock of the center door.]

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [From the next room.] It's unlocked.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: I'm coming.

[She unbolts the door on her side, and goes into Avonia's room, shutting the door behind her. The lid of the dress-basket is open, showing the contents; a pair of little satin shoes lie at the top. Tom takes up one of the shoes and presses it to his lips. There is a knock at the door. He returns the shoe to the basket, closes the lid, and walks away.]

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Yes?
[The door opens slightly and Imogen is heard.]

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: [Outside.] Is that you, Wrench?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Hullo!
[Imogen, in out-of-door costume, enters breathlessly.]

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: [Closing the door—speaking rapidly and excitedly.] Mossop said you were in Rose's room——

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Shaking hands with her.] She'll be here in a few minutes.

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: It's you I want. Let me sit down.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Going to the armchair.] Here——

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: [Sitting on the right of the table, panting.] Not near the fire——

div.head: Tom.
div.p: What's up?

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Oh, Wrench! p'r'aps my fortune's made!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Quite calmly.] Congratulate you, Jenny.

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Do be quiet; don't make such a racket. You see, things haven't been going at all satisfactorily at the Olympic lately. There's Miss Puddifant——

div.head: Tom.
div.p: I know—no lady.

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: How do you know?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Guessed.

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Quite right; and a thousand other annoyances. And at last I took it into my head to consult Mr. Clandon, who married an aunt of mine and lives at Streatham, and he'll lend me five hundred pounds.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: What for?

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Towards taking a theatre.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Dubiously.] Five hundred——

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: It's all he's good for, and he won't advance that unless I can get a further five, or eight, hundred from some other quarter.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: What theatre!

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: The Pantheon happens to be empty.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Yes; it's been that for the last twenty years.

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Don't throw wet blankets—I mean—[referring to her tablets, which she carries in her muff] I've got it all worked out in black and white. There's a deposit required on account of rent—two hundred pounds. Cleaning the theatre—[looking at Tom] what do you say?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Cleaning that theatre?

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: I say, another two hundred.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: That would remove the top-layer——-

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Cost of producing the opening play, five hundred pounds. Balance for emergencies, three hundred. You generally have a balance for emergencies.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: You generally have the emergencies, if not the balance?

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Now, the question is, will five hundred produce the play?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: What play?

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Your play.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Quietly.] My——.

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Your comedy.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Turning to the fire—in a low voice.] Rubbish!

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Well, Mr. Clandon thinks it isn't. [He faces her sharply.] I gave it to him to read, and he—well, he's quite taken with it.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Walking about, his hands in his pockets, his head down, agitatedly.]Clandon—Landon—what's his name——-?

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Tony Clandon—Anthony Clandon——

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Choking.] He's a—he's a—-

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: He's a hop-merchant.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: No, he's not—[sitting on the sofa, leaning his head on his hands] he's a stunner.

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: [Rising] So you grasp the position. Theatre—manageress—author—play, found; and eight hundred pounds wanted!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Rising.] Oh Lord!

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Who's got it?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Wildly.] The Queen's got it! Miss Burdett-Coutts has got it!

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Don't be a fool, Wrench. Do you remember old Mr. Morfew, of Duncan Terrace? He used to take great interest in us all at the "Wells." He has money.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: He has gout; we don't see him now.

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Gout! How lucky! That means he's at home. Will you run round to Duncan Terrace——?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Looking down at his clothes.] I!

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Nonsense, Wrench; we're not asking him to advance money on your clothes.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: The clothes are the man, Jenny.

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: And the woman———?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: The face is the woman; there's the real inequality of the sexes.

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: I'll go! Is my face good enough?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Enthusiastically.] I should say so!

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: [Taking his hands.] Ha, ha! It has been in my possession longer than you have had your oldest coat, Tom!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Make haste, Jenny!

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: [Running up to the door.] Oh, it will last till I get to Duncan Terrace. [Turning.] Tom, you may have to read your play to Mr. Morfew. Have you another copy? Uncle Clandon has mine.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Holding his head.] I think I have—-I don't know——-

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Look for it! Find it! If Morfew wants to hear it, we must strike while the iron's hot.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: While the gold's hot!

div.head: Imogen. and Tom.
div.p: Ha, ha, ha!
[Mrs. Mossop enters, showing some signs of excitement.]

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: [Pushing her aside.] Oh, get out of the way, Mrs. Mossop—- [Imogen departs.]

div.head: Mrs. Mossop.
div.p: Upon my——! [To Tom.] A visitor for Miss Trelawny! Where's Miss Trelawny?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: With Mrs. Gadd. Mossop!

div.head: Mrs. Mossop.
div.p: Don't bother me now——-

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Mossop! The apartments vacated by the Tefferl's. Dare to let 'em without giving me the preference.

div.head: Mrs. Mossop.
div.p: You!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Seizing her hands and swinging her round.] I may be wealthy, sweet Rebecca![Embracing her.] I may be rich and honored!

div.head: Mrs. Mossop.
div.p: Oh, have done! [Releasing herself.] My lodgers do take such liberties——

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [At the door, grandly.] Beccy, half a scuttle of coal, to start with.
[He goes out, leaving the door slightly open.]

div.head: Mrs. Mossop.
div.p: [Knocking at the center door.] Miss Trelawny, my dear! Miss Trelawny!
[The door opens, a few inches.]

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Looking out.] Why, what a clatter you and Mr. Wrench have been making———-!

div.head: Mrs. Mossop.
div.p: [Beckoning her mysteriously.] Come here, dear.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Closing the center door, and entering the room wonderingly.] Eh?

div.head: Mrs. Mossop.
div.p: [In awe.] Sir William Gower!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Sir William.

div.head: Mrs. Mossop.
div.p: Don't be vexed with me. "I'll see if she's at home," I said. "Oh, yes, woman, Miss Trelawny's at home," said he, and hobbled straight in. I've shut him in the Telfers' room——
[There are three distinct raps, with a stick, at the right-hand door.]

div.head: Rose. and Mrs. Mossop.
div.p: Oh-h!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Faintly.] Open it.
[Mrs. Mossop opens the door, and Sir William enters. He is feebler, more decrepit, than when last seen. He wears a plaid about his shoulders and walks with the aid of a stick.]

div.head: Mrs. Mossop.
div.p: [At the door.] Ah, and a sweet thing Miss Trelawny is——!

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Turning to her.] Are you a relative?

div.head: Mrs. Mossop.
div.p: No, I am not a relative——!

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Go. [She departs; he closes the door with the end of his stick. Facing Rose.] My mind is not commonly a wavering one, Miss Trelawny, but it has taken me some time—months—to decide upon calling on ye.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Won't you sit down?

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [After a pause of hesitation, sitting upon the dress-basket.] Ugh!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [With quiet dignity.] Have we no chairs? Do we lack chairs here, Sir William?
[He gives her a quick, keen look, then rises and walks to the fire.]

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Suddenly, bringing his stick down upon the table with violence.] My grandson! my grandson! where is he?

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Arthur!

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: I had but one.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Isn't he—in Cavendish Square—?

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Isn't he in Cavendish Square! no, he is not in Cavendish Square, as you know well.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Oh, I don't know——

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Tsch!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: When did he leave you?

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Tsch!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: When?

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: He made his escape during the night, 22d of August last—[pointing his finger at her] as you know well.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Sir William. I assure you—-

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Tsch! [Talcing off his gloves.] How often does he write to ye?

div.head: Rose.
div.p: He does not write to me. He did write day after day, two or three times a day, for about a week. That was in June, when I came back here. [With drooping head.] He never writes now.

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Visits ye——?

div.head: Rose.
div.p: No.

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Comes troubadouring——-?

div.head: Rose.
div.p: No, no, no. I have not seen him since that night.
I refused to see him———[With a catch in her breath.] Why, he may be——!

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Fumbling in his pocket.] Ah, but he's not. He's alive [producing a small packet of letters]. Arthur's alive, [advancing to her] and full of his tricks still. His great-aunt Trafalgar receives a letter from him once a fortnight, posted in London——

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Holding out her hand for the letters.] Oh!

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Putting them behind his back.] Hey!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Faintly.] I thought you wished me to read them. [He yields them to her grudgingly, she taking his hand and bending over it.] Ah, thank you.

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Withdrawing his hand with a look of disrelish.] What are ye doing, madam? what are ye doing?
[He sits, producing his snuff-box; she sits, upon the basket, facing him, and opens the packet of letters.]

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Reading a letter.] "To reassure you as to my well-being, I cause this to be posted in London by a friend——"

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Pointing a finger at her again, accusingly.] A friend!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Looking up, with simple pride.] He would never call me that. [Reading.] "I am in good bodily health, and as contented as a man can be who has lost the woman he loves, and will love till his dying day—" Ah——!

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Read no more! Return them to me! give them to me, ma'am! [Rising, she restores the letters, meekly. He peers up into her face.] What's come to ye? You are not so much of a vixen as you were.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Shaking her head.] No.

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Suspiciously. ] Less of the devil—?

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: I am sorry for having been a vixen, and for all my unruly conduct, in Cavendish Square. I humbly beg your, and Miss Gower's, forgiveness.

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Taking snuff, uncomfortably.]Pi—i—i—sh! extraordinary change.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Aren't you changed, Sir William, now that you have lost him?

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Don't you love him now, the more? [His head droops a little, and his hands wander to the brooch which secures his plaid.] Let me take your shawl from you. You would catch cold when you go out——
[He allows her to remove the plaid, protesting during the process.]

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: I'll not trouble ye, ma'am. Much obleeged to ye, but I'll not trouble ye. [Rising.] I'll not trouble ye—-

[He walks away to the fireplace, and up the room. She folds the plaid and lays it upon the sofa. He looks round—speaking in an altered tone.] My dear, gypsying doesn't seem to be such a good trade with ye, as it used to be by all accounts——
[The center door opens and Avonia enters boldly, in the dress of a burlesque prince—cotton-velvet shirt, edged with bullion trimming, a cap, white tights, ankle boots, etc.]

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Unconsciously.] How's this, Rose———?

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Ah—h-h—h!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Oh, go away, 'Vonia!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Sir Gower! [To Sir William.] Good-morning.
[She withdraws.]

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Pacing the room—again very violent.] Yes! and these are the associates you would have tempted my boy—my grandson—to herd with! [Flourishing his stick.] Ah—h—h—h!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Sitting upon the basket—weakly.] That young lady doesn't live in that attire. She is preparing for the pantomime———

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Standing over her.] And now he's gone; lured away, I suspect, by one of ye—[pointing to the center door] by one of these harridans!——
[Avonia reappears defiantly.]

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Look here, Sir Gower———

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Rising.] Go, 'Vonia!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [To Sir William.] We've met before, if you remember, in Cavendish Square——

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Sitting again, helplessly.] Oh, Mrs. Gadd——!

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Mistress! a married lady!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Yes, I spent some of my honeymoon at your house——

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: What!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: Excuse my dress; it's all in the way of my business. Just one word about Rose.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Please, 'Vonia——!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [To Sir William, who is glaring at her in horror.] Now, there's nothing to stare at, Sir Gower. If you must look anywhere in particular, look at that poor thing. A nice predicament you've brought her to!

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Sir——! [Correcting himself.]. Madam!

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: You've brought her to beggary, amongst you. You've broken her heart; and, what's worse, you've made her genteel. She can't act, since she left your mansion; she can only mope about the stage with her eyes fixed like a person in a dream—dreaming of him, I suppose, and of what it is to be a lady. And first she's put upon half-salary; and then, to-day, she gets the sack—the entire sack, Sir Gower! So there's nothing left for her but to starve, or to make artificial flowers. Miss Trelawny I'm speaking of! [Going to Rose, and embracing her.] Our Rose! our Trelawny! [To Rose, breaking down.] Excuse me for interfering, ducky. [Retiring, in tears.] Good-day, Sir Gower. [She goes out.]

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [After a pause, to Rose.] Is this—the case?

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Standing, and speaking in a low voice.] Yes. As you have noticed, fortune has turned against me, rather.

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Penitently.] I—I'm sorry, ma'am. I—I believe ye've kept your word to us concerning Arthur. I-I——

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Not heeding him, looking before her, dreamily.'] My mother knew how fickle fortune could be to us gypsies. One of the greatest actors that ever lived warned her of that—-

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Miss Gower will also feel extremely—extremely——

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Kean once warned mother of that.

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [In an altered tone.] Kean? which Kean?

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Edmund Kean. My mother acted with Edmund Kean when she was a girl.

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Approaching her slowly, speaking in a queer voice.] With Kean? with Kean!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Yes.

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [At her side, in a whisper.] My dear, I—I've seen Edmund Kean.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Yes?

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: A young man then, I was; quite different, from the man I am now—impulsive, excitable. Kean! [Drawing a deep breath.] Ah, he was a splendid gypsy!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Looking down at the dress-basket.] I've a little fillet in there that my mother wore as Cordelia to Kean's Lear——

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: I may have seen your mother also. I was somewhat different in those days——

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Kneeling at the basket and opening it.] And the Order and chain, and the sword, he wore in Richard. He gave them to my father; I've always prized them. [She drags to the surface a chain with an Order attached to it, and a sword-belt and sword—all very theatrical and tawdry—and a little gold fillet. She hands him the chain.] That's the Order.

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Handling it tenderly.] Kean! God bless me!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Holding up the fillet.] My poor mother's fillet.

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Looking at it] I may have seen her. [Thoughtfully.] I was a young man then. [Looking at Rose steadily.]Put it on, my dear.
[She goes to the mirror and puts on the fillet.]

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Examining the Order.] Lord bless us! how he stirred me! how he——!
[He puts the chain over his shoulders. Rose turns to him.]

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Advancing to him.] There!

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Looking at her.] Cordelia! Cordelia—with Kean!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Adjusting the chain upon him.] This should hang so. [Returning to the basket and taking up the sword-belt and sword.] Look!

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Handling them.] Kean! [To her, in a whisper.] I'll tell ye! I'll tell ye! when I saw him as Richard—I was young and a fool—I'll tell ye—he almost fired me with an ambition to—to——[Fumbling with the belt.] How did he carry this?

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Fastening the belt, with the sword, round him.] In this way—

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Ah! [He paces the stage, growling and muttering, and walking with a limp and one shoulder hunched. She watches him, seriously.] Ah! he was a little man too! I remember him! as if it were last night!
I remember——- [Pausing and looking at her fixedly.] My dear, your prospects in life have been injured by your unhappy acquaintanceship with my grandson.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Gazing into the fire.] Poor Arthur's prospects in life—what of them?

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Testily.] Tsch, tsch, tsch!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: If I knew where he is——!

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Miss Trelawny, if you cannot act, you cannot earn your living.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: How is he earning his living?

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: And if you cannot earn your living, you must be provided for.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Turning to him.] Provided for?

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Miss Gower was kind enough to bring me here in a cab. She and I will discuss plans for making provision for ye while driving home.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Advancing to him.] Oh, I beg you will do no such thing, Sir William.

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Hey!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: I could not accept any help from you or Miss Gower.

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: You must! you shall!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: I will not.

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Touching the Order and the sword.] Ah!—yes, I—I'll buy these of ye, my dear——

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Oh, no, no! not for hundreds of pounds! please take them off!
[There is a hurried knocking at the door.]

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Startled.] Who's that? [Struggling with the chain and belt.] Remove these———!
[The handle is heard to rattle. Sir William disappears behind the curtains. Imogen opens the door and looks in.]

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: [Seeing only Rose, and coming to her and embracing her.] Rose darling, where is Tom Wrench?

div.head: Rose.
div.p: He was here not long since——

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: [Going to the door and calling, desperately.] Tom! Tom Wrench! Mr. Wrench!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Is anything amiss?

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: [Shrilly.] Tom!

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Imogen!

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: [Returning to Rose.] Oh, my dear, forgive my agitation—-!
[Tom enters, buoyantly, flourishing the manuscript of his play.]

div.head: Tom.
div.p: I've found it! at the bottom of a box—"deeper than did ever plummet sound——"! [To Imogen.]
Eh? what's the matter?

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Oh, Tom, old Mr. Morfew——-!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Blankly.] Isn't he willing—-?

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: [With a gesture of despair.] I don't know. He's dead.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: No!

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Three weeks ago. Oh, what a chance he has missed!
[Tom bangs his manuscript down upon the table savagely.]

div.head: Rose.
div.p: What is it, Tom? Imogen, what is it?

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: [Pacing the room.] I can think of no one else——

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Done again!

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: We shall lose it, of course—

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Lose what?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: The opportunity—her opportunity, my opportunity, your opportunity, Rose.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Coming to him.] My opportunity, Tom?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Pointing to the manuscript.] My play—my comedy—my youngest born! Jenny has a theatre—could have one—has five hundred towards it, put down by a man who believes in my comedy, God bless him!—the only fellow who has ever believed——?

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Oh, Tom! [turning to Imogen] oh, Imogen!

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: My dear, five hundred! we want another five, at least.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Another five!

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Or eight.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: And you are to play the part of Dora. Isn't she, Jenny—I mean, wasn't she?

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Certainly. Just the sort of simple little Miss you could play now, Rose. And we thought that old Mr. Morfew would help us in the speculation. Speculation! it's a dead certainty!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Dead certainty? poor Morfew!

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: And here we are, stuck fast——!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Sitting upon the dress-basket dejectedly.] And they'll expect me to rehearse that dragon to-morrow with enthusiasm.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Putting her arm around his shoulder.] Never mind, Tom.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: No, I won't——[Taking her hand.] Oh,

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Looking up at her.]Oh, Dora——!
[Sir William, divested of his theatrical trappings, comes from behind the curtain.]

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Oh! Tom. [Rising.] Eh?

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Retreating]. Sir William Gower, Tom——

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [To Tom.] I had no wish to be disturbed, sir, and I withdrew [bowing to Imogen] when that lady entered the room. I have been a party, it appears, to a consultation upon a matter of business. [To Tom.] Do I understand, sir, that you have been defeated in some project which would have served the interests of Miss Trelawny.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Y—y—yes, sir.

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Mr. Wicks

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Wrench——

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Tsch! Sir, it would give me pleasure—it would give my grandson, Mr. Arthur Gower, pleasure—to be able to aid Miss Trelawny at the present moment.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: S—s—sir William, w—w—would you like to hear my play——?

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Sharply.] Hey! [Looking round.] Ho, ho!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: My comedy?

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Cunningly.] So ye think I might be induced to fill the office ye designed for the late Mr.— Mr. ————

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Morfew.

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Morfew, eh?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: N—n—no, sir.

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: No! no!

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: [Shrilly.] Yes!

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [After a short pause, quietly.] Read your play, sir. [Pointing to a chair at the table.] Sit down. [To Rose and Imogen.] Sit down.
[Tom goes to the chair indicated. Miss Gower's voice is heard outside the door.]

div.head: Miss Gower.
div.p: [Outside.] William! [Rose opens the door; Miss Gower enters.] Oh, William, what has become of you? has anything dreadful happened?

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Sit down, Trafalgar. This gentleman is about to read a comedy. A cheer! [Testily.] Are there no cheers here! [Rose brings a chair and places it for Miss Gower beside Sir William's chair.] Sit down.

div.head: Miss Gower.
div.p: [Sitting, bewildered.] William, is all this—quite——?

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Sitting.] Yes, Trafalgar, quite in place—quite in place——
[Imogen sits. Rose pulls the dress-basket round, as Colpoys and Gadd swagger in at the door, Colpoys smoking a pipe, Gadd a large cigar.]

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [To Tom, referring to Gadd and Colpoys.] Friends of yours?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Yes, Sir William.

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [To Gadd and Colpoys.] Sit down. [Imperatively.] Sit down and be silent.
[Gadd and Colpoys seat themselves upon the sofa, like men in a dream. Rose sits on the dress-basket.]

div.head: Avonia.
div.p: [Opening the center door slightly—in an anxious voice.] Rose——!

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: Come in, ma'am, come in! [Avonia enters, coming to Rose. A cloak is now attached to the shoulders of Avonia's dress.] Sit down, ma'am, and be silent!
[Avonia sits beside Rose, next to Miss Gower.]

div.head: Miss Gower.
div.p: [In horror.] Oh—h—h—h!

div.head: Sir William.
div.p: [Restraining her.] Quite in place, Trafalgar; quite in place. [To Tom.] Now, sir!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Opening his manuscript and reading.] "Life, a comedy, by Thomas Wrench——"

div.head: THE FOURTH ACT.

p.hi: The scene represents the stage of a theatre with the proscenium arch, and the dark and empty auditorium in the distance. The curtain is raised. The stage extends a few feet beyond the line of the proscenium, and is terminated by a row of old-fashioned footlights with metal reflectors. On the left, from the proscenium arch runs a wall, in which is an open doorway supposed to admit to the Green-room. Right and left of the stage are the "P." and "O. P." and the first and second entrances, with wings running in grooves, according to the old fashion. Against the wall are some "flats." Just below the footlights is a T-light, burning gas, and below this the prompt-table. On the right of the prompt-table is a chair, and on the left another. Against the edge of the proscenium arch is another chair; and nearer, on the right, stands a large throne-chair, with a gilt frame and red velvet seat, now much dilapidated. In the "second entrance" there are a "property" stool, a table, and a chair, all of a similar style to the throne-chair and in like condition, and on the center, as if placed therefor the purpose of rehearsal, are a small circular table and a chair. On this table is a work-basket containing a ball of wool and a pair of knitting-needles; and on the prompt-table there is a book. A faded and ragged green baize covers the floor of the stage. The wings, and the flats and borders, suggest by their appearance a theatre fallen somewhat into decay. The light is a dismal one, but it is relieved by a shaft of' sunlight entering through a window in the flies on the right.

div.p: [Mrs. Telfer is seated upon the throne-chair, in an attitude of dejection. Telfer enters from the Green-room.]

div.head: Telfer.
div.p: [Coming to her.] Is that you, Violet?

div.head: Mrs. Telfer.
div.p: Is the reading over?

div.head: Telfer.
div.p: Almost. My part is confined to the latter 'alf of the second act; so being close to the Green-room door [with a sigh], I stole away.

div.head: Mrs. Telfer.
div.p: It affords you no opportunity, James?

div.head: Telfer.
div.p: [Shaking his head.] A mere fragment.

div.head: Mrs. Telfer.
div.p: [Rising.]Well, but a few good speeches to a man of your stamp——

div.head: Telfer.
div.p: Yes, but this is so line-y, Violet; so very line-y. And what d'ye think the character is described as?

div.head: Mrs. Telfer.
div.p: What?

div.head: Telfer.
div.p: "An old, stagey, out-of-date actor."
[They stand looking at each other for a moment, silently.]

div.head: Mrs. Telfer.
div.p: [Falteringly.] Will you—be able—to get near it, James?

div.head: Telfer.
div.p: [Looking away from her.] I dare say——-

div.head: Mrs. Telfer.
div.p: [Laying a hand upon his shoulder.] That's all right, then.

div.head: Telfer.
div.p: And you—what have they called you for, if you're not in the play? They 'ave not dared to suggest understudy?

div.head: Mrs. Telfer.
div.p: [Playing with her fingers.]They don't ask me to act at all, James.

div.head: Telfer.
div.p: Don't ask you—-!

div.head: Mrs. Telfer.
div.p: Miss Parrott offers me the position of Wardrobe-mistress.

div.head: Telfer.
div.p: Violet!

div.head: Mrs. Telfer.
div.p: Hush!

div.head: Telfer.
div.p: Let us both go home.

div.head: Mrs. Telfer.
div.p: [Restraining him.] No, let us remain. We've been idle six months, and I can't bear to see you without your watch and all your comforts about you.

div.head: Telfer.
div.p: [Pointing toward the Green-room.] And so this new-fangled stuff, and these dandified people, are to push us, and such as us, from our stools!

div.head: Mrs. Telfer.
div.p: Yes, James, just as some other new fashion will, in course of time, push them from their stools.

[From the Green-room comes the sound of a slight clapping of hands, followed by a murmur of voices. The Telfers move away. Imogen, elaborately dressed, enters from the Green-room and goes leisurely to the prompt-table. She is followed by Tom, manuscript in hand, smarter than usual in appearance; and he by O'Dwyer,—an excitable Irishman of about forty, with an extravagant head of hair,—who carries a small bundle of "parts" in brown-paper covers. Tom and O'Dwyer join Imogen.]

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: [To Tom.] Mr. Wrench, I congratulate ye; I have that honor, sir. Your piece will do, sir; it will take the town, mark me.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Thank you, O'Dwyer.

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Look at the sunshine! there's a good omen, at any rate.

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: Oh, sunshine's nothing. [To Tom.] But did ye observe the gloom on their faces whilst ye were read in'?

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: [Anxiously.] Yes, they did look glum.

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: Glum! it might have been a funeral! There's a healthy prognostication for ye, if ye loike! it's infallible.
[A keen-faced gentleman and a lady enter, from the Green-room, and stroll across the stage to the right, where they lean against the wings and talk. Then two young gentlemen enter, and Rose follows.]
Note.—The actors and the actress appearing for the first time in this act, as members of the Pantheon Company, are outwardly greatly superior to the Gadds, the Telfers, and Colpoys.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [Shaking hands with Telfer.] Why didn't you sit near me, Mr. Telfer? [Going to Mrs. Telfer.] Fancy our being together again, and at the West End! [To Telfer.] Do you like the play?

div.head: Telfer.
div.p: Like it! there's not a speech in it, my dear—not a real speech; nothing to dig your teeth into—-

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: [Allotting the parts, under the direction of Tom and Imogen.] Mr. Mortimer! [One of the young gentlemen advances and receives his part from O'Dwyer, and retires, reading it.] Mr. Denzil!
[The keen-faced gentleman takes his part, then joins Imogen on her left and talks to her. The lady now has something to say to the solitary young gentleman.]

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [To O'Dwyer, quietly, handing him a part.] Miss Brewster.

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: [Beckoning to the lady, who does not observe him, her back being towards him.] Come here, my love.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [To O'Dwyer.] No, no, O'Dwyer—not your "love."

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: [Perplexed.] Not?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: No.

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: No?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Why, you are meeting her this morning for the first time.

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: That's true enough. [Approaching the lady and handing her the part.] Miss Brewster.

div.head: The Lady.
div.p: Much obliged.

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: [Quietly to her.] It 'll fit ye like a glove, darlin'. [The lady sits, conning her part. O'Dwyer returns to the table.]

div.head: Telfer.
div.p: [To Rose.] Your lover in the play? which of these young sparks plays your lover—Harold or Gerald——?

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Gerald. I don't know. There are some people not here to-day, I believe.

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: Mr. Hunston!
[The second young gentleman advances, receives his part, and joins the other young gentleman in the wings.]

div.head: Rose.
div.p: Not that young man, I hope. Isn't he a little bandy?

div.head: Telfer.
div.p: One of the finest Macduffs I ever fought with was bow-legged.

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: Mr. Teller.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [To O'Dwyer.] No, no—Telfer.

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: Telfer!
[Telfer draws himself erect, puts his hand in his breast, but otherwise remains stationary.]

div.head: Mrs. Telfer.
div.p: [Anxiously.] That's you, James.

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: Come on, Mr. Telfer! look alive, sir!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [To O'Dwyer.] Sssh, sssh, sssh! don't, don't——!

[Telfer advances to the prompt-table, slowly. He receives his part from O'Dwyer. To Telfer, awkwardly.] I—I hope the little part of Poggs appeals to you, Mr. Telfer. Only a sketch, of course; but there was nothing else—quite—in your———-

div.head: Telfer.
div.p: Nothing? to whose share does the Earl fall?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Oh; Mr. Denzil plays Lord Parracourt.

div.head: Telfer.
div.p: Denzil? I've never 'eard of 'im. Will you get to me to-day?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: We—we expect to do so.

div.head: Telfer.
div.p: Very well. [Stiffly.] Let me be called in the street. [He stalks away.]

div.head: Mrs. Telfer.
div.p: [Relieved.] Thank Heaven! I was afraid James would break out.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: [To Mrs. Telfer.] But you, dear Mrs. Telfer—you weren't at the reading—what are you cast for?

div.head: Mrs. Telfer.
div.p: I? [Wiping away a tear.] I am the Wardrobe-mistress of this theatre.

div.head: Rose.
div.p: You! [Embracing her.] Oh! oh!

div.head: Mrs. Telfer.
div.p: [Composing herself.] Miss Trelawny—Rose—my child, if we are set to scrub a floor—and we may come to that yet—let us make up our minds to scrub it legitimately—with dignity——
[She disappears and is seen no more.]

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: Miss Trelawny! come here, my de——

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [To O'Dwyer.] Hush!

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: Miss Trelawny!

[Rose receives her part from O'Dwyer and, after a word or two with Tom and Imogen, joins the two young gentlemen who are in the "second entrance, L." The lady, who has been seated, now rises and crosses to the left, where she meets the keen-faced gentleman, who has finished his conversation with Imogen.]

div.head: The Lady.
div.p: [To the keen-faced gentleman.] I say, Mr. Denzil! who plays Gerald?

div.head: The Gentlemen.
div.p: Gerald?

div.head: The Lady.
div.p: The man I have my scene with in the third act—the hero—-

div.head: The Gentleman.
div.p: Oh, yes. Oh, a young gentleman from the country, I understand.

div.head: The Lady.
div.p: From the country!

div.head: The Gentleman.
div.p: He is coming up by train this morning, Miss Parrott tells me; from Bath or somewhere—-

div.head: The Lady.
div.p: Well, whoever he is, if he can't play that scene with me decently, my part's not worth rags.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [To Imogen, who is sitting at the prompt-table.] Er—h'm—shall we begin, Miss Parrott?

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Certainly, Mr. Wrench.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: We'll begin, O'Dwyer.
[The lady titters at some remark from the keen-faced gentleman.]

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: [Coming down the stage, violently.] Clear the stage there! I'll not have it! Upon my honor, this is the noisiest theatre I've ever set foot in!
[The icings are cleared, the characters disappearing into the Green-room.]

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: I can't hear myself speak for all the riot and confusion!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [To O'Dwyer.] My dear O'Dwyer, there is no riot, there is no confusion—

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: [To O'Dwyer.] Except the riot and confusion you are making.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: You know, you're admirably earnest, O'Dwyer, but a little excitable.

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: [Calming himself.] Oh, I beg your pardon, I'm sure. [Emphatically.] My system is, begin as you mean to go on.

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: But we don't mean to go on like that.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Of course not; of course not. Now, let me see—[pointing to the right center] we shall want another chair here.

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: Another chair?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: A garden chair.

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: [Excitably.] Another chair! Now, then, another chair! Properties! where are ye? do ye hear me callin'? must I raise my voice to ye-?
[He rushes away.]

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: [To Tom.] Phew! where did you get him from? Tom.
[Wiping his brow.] Known Michael for years—most capable, invaluable fellow——

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: [Simply.] I wish he was dead.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: So do I.
[O'Dwyer returns, carrying a light chair.]

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Well, where's the property-man?

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: [Pleasantly.] It's all right now. He's gone to dinner.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: [Placing the chair in position.] Ah, then he'll be back some time during the afternoon. [Looking about him.] That will do. [Taking up his manuscript.] Call—haven't you engaged a call-boy yet, O'Dwyer?

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: I have, sir, and the best in London.

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Where is he?

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: He has sint an apology for his non-attindance.

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: Oh!

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: A sad case, ma'am; he's buryin' his wife.

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Wife!

div.head: Imogen.
div.p: The call-boy?

div.head: Tom.
div.p: What's his age?

div.head: O'Dwyer.
div.p: Ye see, he happens to be an elder brother of my own——

div.head: Imogen. and Tom.
div.p: O Lord!

div.head: Tom.
div.p: Nevermind! let's get on! Call Miss—— [Looking toward the right.] Is that the Hall-Keeper?
[A man, suggesting by his appearance that he is the Hall-Keeper, presents himself, with a card in his hand.]

div.head: O'Dwyer.
